questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-1,1]$, where $f$ is $2$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $2$-periodic on $[-1,1]$, we have $L=1$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{5}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{5}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 4 & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=3
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+8y=f(x)
$$

on $[-3,3]$, where $f$ is $6$-periodic and even. What Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution $y_p?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $6$-periodic on $[-3,3]$, we have $L=3$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a cosine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+2y=f(x), \qquad y'(0)=0,\quad y'(1)=-5
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and even. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution $y_p$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution $y_p$ satisfies $y_p'(0) = 0$ and $y_p'(1) = 0.$*
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094598/assets/579150783e9ae1e69686ff319572bf5523934bf8eb266c5c19e9bf553aa8b0e1.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y=y_c+y_p$, where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation $y''+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
y'(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+y_p'(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since $y_p'(0)=0$ and $y_p'(1)=0$, we have

$$
y'(0)=y_c'(0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(1)=y_c'(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y'(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{2}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{2}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y'(1)=-5$ with $B=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ -5 & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ A & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)\sim \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt gray]{\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2})}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)}
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).
$$
